exam: Record BP and temperature — severe hypertension and fever each redirect the work-up
Test neck flexion for stiffness; Kernig's sign if febrile
Perform fundoscopy for papilloedema (raised intracranial pressure) and subhyaloid haemorrhage (SAH)
Check pupils and eye movements — third-nerve palsy with a dilated pupil raises aneurysm
Screen visual fields by confrontation — bitemporal or homonymous defects raise a mass lesion
Palpate the temporal arteries for tenderness, thickening, or absent pulsation (giant cell arteritis)
Press over the frontal and maxillary sinuses and transilluminate if possible (sinusitis)
Test limb power, reflexes, and plantar responses for asymmetry (space-occupying lesion, stroke)
Assess gait and coordination — ataxia points to a posterior fossa lesion
Palpate pericranial and trapezius muscles for tenderness (tension-type)
Examine the scalp and jaw: pain on sustained chewing (jaw claudication) supports arteritis

investigations.why: The decisive first-line test for giant cell arteritis in any new headache over 50 — markedly raised values rule it in as the working diagnosis; normal values make it unlikely; both usually normal in migraine, tension-type, and cluster
Leukocytosis supports meningitis or sinusitis; anaemia of chronic disease accompanies arteritis and malignancy; normal count reassures in primary headaches

investigations.test: Random blood glucose and renal function
investigations.why: Hypoglycaemia is a reversible headache mimic; renal status is required before contrast imaging and interprets severe hypertension found on exam

Second-line, but URGENT when indicated: thunderclap onset (blood of SAH), focal deficit, papilloedema, new headache > 50, progressive daily pattern, or head trauma — rules haemorrhage and mass in or out; NOT needed for a typical migraine or tension pattern with a normal exam

investigations.test: Lumbar puncture (after imaging excludes mass effect)
investigations.why: Rules in meningitis (cells, protein, glucose, culture) in the febrile stiff-necked patient; xanthochromia rules in SAH when CT is normal but the story is thunderclap; opening pressure diagnoses idiopathic intracranial hypertension

investigations.test: Sinus X-ray or limited sinus CT
investigations.why: Air-fluid levels or mucosal thickening support acute sinusitis when facial pressure and postnasal discharge are present; a normal study moves the pain back to migraine, which is often mislabelled as sinus headache
Second-line — preferred over CT for progressively worsening headache with normal CT, suspected posterior fossa lesion (ataxia), or pituitary symptoms; rules structural lesions in or out definitively
